scope: The carriers whole: Dio's orations, the two Plutarch treatises, Stobaeus's third book, and the papyrus volume.
verified_loci: Dio Chrysostom Or. 37.47 (Favorinus): fr. 147, 'finely said by Sappho' — 'μνάσεσθαί τινά φαμι καὶ ἕτερον ἀμμέων. πάνυ γὰρ καλῶς εἶπεν ἡ Σαπφώ'

Dio 37.47: Hesiod on undying report, and the speaker's own statue set up beside the goddess — 'φήμη δ’ οὔτις πάμπαν ἀπόλλυται, ἥντινα λαοὶ πολλοὶ φημίξωσι· θεός νύ τίς ἐστι καὶ αὐτή. ἐγώ σε ἀναστήσω παρὰ τῇ θεῷ'

Plutarch, Coniugalia praecepta 145f–146a: Sappho proud of the καλλιγραφία of her songs, writing to a rich woman — 'διὰ τὴν ἐν τοῖς μέλεσι καλλιγραφίαν ἐφρόνει τηλικοῦτον ὥστε γράψαι πρός τινα πλουσίαν'
Plutarch, Coniugalia praecepta (fr. 55, with the editor's text from 646f): no memory of you — 'κατθανοῦσα δὲ κείσεαι, οὐδέ τις μναμοσύνα σέθεν ἔσεται'
Plutarch, Quaestiones convivales 646e–f: Sappho to an unmusical and unlearned woman — 'μεμνῆσθαί μοι δοκῶ Σαπφοῦς λεγούσης πρός τινα τῶν ἀμούσων καὶ ἀμαθῶν γυναικῶν'
Stobaeus 3.4.12 (Hense): Sappho to an uneducated woman (OCR) — 'Σαπφοῦς πρὸς ἁπαίδευτον γυναῖκα'
P.Oxy. XV 1787: Sappho, Book IV (OCR) — '1787. SAPPHO, BOOK iv.'
P.Oxy. XV 1790 (Ibycus): Polycrates promised imperishable fame (OCR) — 'In the penultimate line the author addresses Polycrates, to whom he ascribes imperishable fame.'
why_seated: The ancient dossier of #1548 Part I §3 in the books that carry it. Dio's Corinthian oration (generally given to Favorinus) quotes fr. 147 with Hesiod on undying report and the speaker's own statue; Plutarch quotes fr. 55, the unremembered woman, and says Sappho was proud of the καλλιγραφία in her songs, enough to write to a rich woman; Stobaeus files the same lines under 'To an uneducated woman'; P.Oxy. XV prints Sappho's fourth book and the Ibycus poem that promises Polycrates imperishable fame. The ancient record holds remembrance claims, and the seat holds them where they stand.
